item.title: DexEngine Converts Human Hand Motions into Robot-Executable Data at Scale
item.description:
DexEngine Converts Human Hand Motions into Robot-Executable Data at Scale

📚 Introduction

A new pipeline called DexEngine has been introduced to convert human hand-object demonstrations into large-scale, physically executable trajectories for training robotic manipulation policies.

🧩 How It Works

DexEngine processes human motion data in three stages:

  • Places each clip’s hand-object motion where robot arms can reach it
  • Finds an arm motion that follows the human hands
  • Corrects the motion in physics simulation using residual reinforcement learning

⚙️ Key Details

The system generates substantial amounts of training data:

Metric Value
Datasets Processed 9 human hand-object datasets
Clips per Hand 5,200
Total Trajectories 65,000 (116 h)
Total Episodes 325,000 (578 h)

Key findings include:

  • Policies trained on data corrected by DexEngine outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with arms attached after a floating-hand correction
  • Fine-tuning on physics-corrected data is essential for performance
  • Mid-training on the generated data provides additional improvements in both simulation and on real robots
  • DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods
  • The pipeline operates more than 10x faster than reinforcement learning-based alternatives

💡 Why It Matters

The research demonstrates that depth coverage is more critical than measurement precision for learned manipulation policies. Additionally, the findings highlight that policies trained on clean depth data lose performance when holes appear during deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These insights suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should be evaluated based on depth coverage rather than measurement precision.

🚀 Availability

The work is classified under Computer Science > Robotics and was submitted on 25 Nov 2026. The paper is available for viewing in PDF and HTML formats.

#Robotics #ImitationLearning #DexEngine #Manipulation #DepthSensing

Source: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT Source: DexEngine: Scaling Human Demonstrations into Physically Executable Whole-Robot Data

item.title: RoboARC benchmarks robot manipulation under precise spatial constraints
item.description:
RoboARC benchmarks robot manipulation under precise spatial constraints

RoboARC is a new benchmark designed to test whether robot agents can reason out the correct motions for hard manipulation tasks that hinge on exact spatial constraints. The collection features 90 tasks across six constraint types, involving both rigid and soft materials, evaluated in MuJoCo simulation on three different robot platforms.

🧩 How it works

Each task is structured as a frozen scene with a physics-based grader and a verified reference solution that replays bit-identically. Tasks are provided in two evaluation regimes:

  • Privileged regime: Full simulator state access and resets allowed
  • Standard regime: Real-sensor inputs (camera images and proprioception) with a single attempt and no resets

Seven coding agents and four vision-language-action (VLA) policies—none trained on these tasks—were evaluated against the benchmark.

⚙️ Key details

The strongest performer was GPT-6 Astra in Codex, which achieved:

  • 86% success rate in the Privileged regime
  • 43% success rate in the Standard regime

The four VLA policies, evaluated zero-shot, solved none of their 18 one-arm puzzles.

Analysis of 15 tasks that GPT-6 Astra solved in Privileged but failed in Standard revealed that:

  • Object poses alone added 4 points (from 24% to 28%)
  • Part geometry alone added 13 points (from 24% to 37%)
  • Both object poses and part geometry together added 36 points (from 24% to 60%)

Only 7% of the coding agents’ failed runs passed more than half of a task, and 53% of failed runs in the Standard regime were stuck on a single step. The results show that frontier coding agents can reason out correct motions once they know object locations and shapes, but performance drops significantly when relying solely on sensor inputs in a single attempt.

🚀 Availability

The RoboARC benchmark is available at the project website.

💡 Why it matters

The findings highlight that spatial constraint understanding remains a critical gap in robotic manipulation. While agents can reason about motion when given complete scene information, real-world sensor limitations significantly reduce performance. The benchmark provides a standardized evaluation framework for future research in constraint-based manipulation tasks.

#robotics #manipulation #benchmark #spatial #AI

item.title: New Robotic Manipulation Methods: RePlan-VLA, LAGR, and GTI
item.description:
New Robotic Manipulation Methods: RePlan-VLA, LAGR, and GTI

Three new approaches address distinct challenges in robotic manipulation: managing long-horizon task execution, selecting task-oriented grasps, and maintaining semantic intent over multiple stages. These methods aim to improve reliability and success rates in complex physical environments by refining how Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and grasping detectors process state and context.

📋 RePlan-VLA: Progress-Aware Replanning

A new framework called RePlan-VLA addresses performance degradation in VLA models on long-horizon tasks involving multiple interdependent manipulations.

  • Core Logic: It leverages the VLA’s existing short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework, rather than burdening the policy with long-horizon reasoning, memory, or error recovery.
  • Mechanism: The framework explicitly monitors robot motion for progress evaluation and adaptively revises the future plan based on observed outcomes.
  • Compatibility: It is VLA-agnostic and preserves the underlying policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning.
  • Performance:
    • Achieves a 21.9% improvement in success rate over the next strongest baseline on the RoboCasa365 benchmark.
    • Achieves a 10.4% improvement on the CALVIN benchmark.
    • Validated for real-world deployment on a Franka Research 3 robot.

🤏 LAGR: Task-Oriented Grasp Detection

The LAGR method and its accompanying dataset address the need for grasps that are both physically feasible and suitable for specific downstream tasks (e.g., holding a hammer by the handle for use vs. the head for handover).

  • Dataset: A newly constructed dataset contains 2.68 million scored 5-DoF grasp annotations across 100,911 image-task pairs from 17 object categories.
  • Architecture:
    1. Generates task-independent grasp proposals with a physical feasibility score.
    2. Uses a language-conditioned re-ranker to score these proposals jointly.
  • Results:
    • Outperforms the next best method by 9.3 percentage points.
    • Validated on real objects using a Franka Research 3 robot.

🎯 GTI: Grounding Task Intent

GTI (Grounding Task Intent) ensures that global task intent remains grounded in the currently executable context during long-horizon manipulation.

  • How it Works: Uses current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase.
  • Visual Targets: For each local subtask, it generates two phase-dependent visual targets:
    • An interaction/contact state.
    • A local completion state.
    • These targets, alongside the local language instruction, jointly condition the VLA to specify both current actions and target states.
  • Recovery: Includes anomaly monitoring and local recovery mechanisms (rollback, re-observation, phase re-evaluation) to re-establish intent consistency after persistent deviation.
  • Performance Gains:
    • RoboCasa365: GR00T success on seen composite tasks increases from 14.6% to 31.8% (Identity Distribution) and from 12.1% to 20.4% (Out-of-Distribution) compared to matched Global-FT baselines.
    • VLA-Arena: GTI + $\pi_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with significant gains on harder L1/L2 tasks.
    • Real-World: Mean full-task success on PiPER tasks increases from 21.7% to 59.2%.

⚙️ Submission Details

All three papers were submitted to arXiv on November 18, 2026.
